notes.meaning: Five days after Paul arrives in Caesarea, High Priest Ananias and several Jewish elders travel down from Jerusalem. They bring a Roman lawyer named Tertullus to lay formal legal charges before Governor Felix. The Jewish leaders hire a professional speaker because they want to use Roman court rules to make sure Paul is condemned.

Tertullus begins his speech by praising Governor Felix with heavy flattery. He thanks Felix for bringing lasting peace and great reforms to the Jewish people everywhere. In reality, Felix was known for being harsh and corrupt, but Roman lawyers often praised judges to win their favor.

Tertullus politely asks Felix to listen for just a short moment so he does not burden the busy governor. He acts humble and respectful to keep Felix in a good mood. His polite words are meant to hide how weak his actual charges against Paul really are.

Tertullus accuses Paul of being a human plague who stirs up riots among Jews across the whole empire. He also calls Paul a leader of the Nazarenes, which was a scornful name for followers of Jesus. He frames Paul as a dangerous political rebel to get the Roman government to step in.

Tertullus claims that Paul tried to desecrate the holy temple, which caused the Jewish leaders to arrest him. He insists they only wanted to put Paul on trial under their own religious law. In truth, an angry crowd had dragged Paul out of the temple and was trying to beat him to death.

Tertullus complains that Commander Lysias arrived with soldiers and took Paul away from them by force. He tries to make Lysias look like an unjust intruder who blocked their legal court. In reality, Lysias had rescued Paul from being murdered without a trial.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Most modern scholars point out that this verse is absent from the oldest and best Greek manuscripts, suggesting it was added by a later copyist.

notes.meaning: Tertullus tells Felix that by questioning Paul directly, the governor can see that all the charges are true. The prosecution offers no outside witnesses or hard proof. They simply hope Paul will say something under questioning that condemns himself.

The Jewish leaders present in the courtroom agree with Tertullus and claim his speech is entirely true. By backing up these claims, they take full responsibility for the false accusations. People often join in wicked lies when they let hatred guide their actions.

Felix motions for Paul to speak, and Paul begins his defense with calm confidence. Paul avoids fake flattery, but politely notes that Felix has governed the province for several years and understands Jewish matters well. Knowing his judge is experienced gives Paul hope for a fair hearing.

Paul points out that it has only been twelve days since he arrived in Jerusalem to worship God. That short time could easily be checked by witnesses. It left him no time to build a political movement or plan an uprising.

Paul states that no one ever saw him arguing in the temple or stirring up a crowd in the synagogues or city streets. He directly challenges his accusers to bring actual proof for any of their claims. False charges quickly fall apart when there is no real evidence to support them.

Paul admits that he follows the Way, which his accusers call a breakaway sect, but insists he worships the same God his ancestors served. He explains that his Christian faith is rooted in the Scriptures, because he believes everything written in the Jewish Law and Prophets. True faith in Christ fulfills God's ancient promises rather than destroying them.

Paul explains that he shares the hope held by most Jews that God will raise the dead to life again. This future resurrection will include both the righteous, who are saved by God, and the wicked, who rejected Him. Because all people will rise, everyone must one day stand before God for final judgment.

Because Paul lives with the coming resurrection in mind, he works constantly to keep a clear conscience before God and people. A clear conscience means obeying God's commands and dealing honestly with others so that nothing brings guilt or blame. Knowing that God sees everything inspires believers to live upright lives.

Paul explains that after several years away, he came to Jerusalem to bring alms, which were charitable gifts of money for the poor, as well as religious offerings. He returned to bless his people and honor God, not to stir up trouble. His real actions proved his deep love and respect for his nation.

Paul reminds Felix that when his enemies found him in the temple, he was ritually pure and quiet, without any mob or disturbance. He points out that the Asian Jews who actually caused the riot ought to be in court to testify if they had real evidence against him. In Roman justice, charges could not stand without the actual eyewitnesses present.

Paul challenges the leaders standing before Felix to state any crime they found in him during his hearing before their council. The only thing he had done was cry out that he was on trial for believing in the resurrection of the dead. That statement was not a crime, but a core belief of Jewish Scripture.

Felix already knows quite a bit about the Christian movement, called the Way, and sees that Paul has committed no crime. Instead of releasing him, Felix puts off the decision by claiming he must wait until Commander Lysias comes down to Caesarea. Delaying justice was an easy way for an unjust ruler to avoid offending the Jewish leaders.

Felix places Paul in the custody of a centurion but orders that he be granted generous personal freedom. He instructs the guard not to stop Paul's friends from visiting him and bringing him food and supplies. This relaxed confinement showed that Felix knew Paul was not a violent criminal.

A few days later, Felix returns with his wife Drusilla, who was a Jewish princess, and calls for Paul to hear him talk about faith in Christ Jesus. Drusilla had deserted her previous husband to marry Felix, and both were curious about this new teaching. Paul treats the meeting as an opportunity to share the gospel with rulers.

Paul speaks boldly about living right, controlling one's desires, and facing God's future judgment, which terrifies Felix. Felix cuts the meeting short and sends Paul away, promising to call for him when a convenient time comes. Putting off repentance when God's truth hits home is a dangerous trap.

differ.view: Methodists stress that Felix missed a real opportunity for salvation, warning that putting off conviction hardens the heart so that a convenient season never arrives.
Calvinistic Baptists teach that the Spirit's restraining grace awakened Felix's conscience and caused natural fear of judgment, but without saving grace his heart remained unchanged.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The traditional Catholic reading translates self-control here as chastity, seeing Paul's message as a direct rebuke of the unlawful marriage between Felix and Drusilla.

notes.meaning: Felix sends for Paul often to talk with him, hoping Paul or his friends will pay a bribe for his release. Paul refuses to buy his freedom, choosing prison over corruption. Felix's love of money blinds him to the spiritual message he heard.

Two full years pass while Paul remains held in Caesarea, until Porcius Festus arrives as the new governor. Felix is recalled to Rome, and to stay on good terms with the angry Jewish leaders, he leaves Paul locked up. Corrupt leaders often sacrifice innocent people just to protect their own reputations.
